title: Euthydemus: Socrates shows true exhortation to wisdom against eristic word-play
summary: Socrates contrasts the sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, who trap a boy with verbal tricks, with his own sincere exhortation to philosophy. He argues that no possession is good unless guided by wisdom, so wisdom is the only good and ignorance the only evil. The search for the knowledge that both makes and uses ends in perplexity, yet he urges Crito to pursue philosophy itself, not judge it by bad teachers.

principles.text: Everyone desires happiness, and happiness comes from the right use of goods, which only knowledge can guide.
principles.quote: Seeing that all men desire happiness, and happiness, as has been shown, is gained by a use, and a right use, of the things of life, and the right use of them, and good-fortune in the use of them, is given by knowledge

principles.text: Wealth, health and the like are neither good nor bad in themselves; wisdom makes them good, ignorance makes them evil.
principles.quote: the goods of which we spoke before are not to be regarded as goods in themselves, but the degree of good and evil in them depends on whether they are or are not under the guidance of knowledge

principles.text: Wisdom is the only true good and ignorance the only evil, so everyone should try to become as wise as possible.
principles.quote: Is not this the result--that other things are indifferent, and that wisdom is the only good, and ignorance the only evil?

principles.text: Merely possessing good things profits nothing; they must be used, and used rightly.
principles.quote: a man who would be happy must not only have the good things, but he must also use them; there is no advantage in merely having them?

principles.text: Verbal trickery with word meanings is play, not wisdom; knowing it makes no one wiser.
principles.quote: if a man had all that sort of knowledge that ever was, he would not be at all the wiser; he would only be able to play with men, tripping them up and oversetting them with distinctions of words.

principles.text: Judge philosophy by itself, not by its bad teachers; every craft has many poor practitioners and few excellent ones.
principles.quote: do not mind whether the teachers of philosophy are good or bad, but think only of philosophy herself. Try and examine her well and truly
